what.text: MOTS-c is a chain of 16 amino acids: Met-Arg-Trp-Gln-Glu-Met-Gly-Tyr-Ile-Phe-Tyr-Pro-Arg-Lys-Leu-Arg. Its molecular weight is about 2,175 daltons. Products are made synthetically and sold as a free base or an acetate salt. It is a common name, not an official drug name.
The body makes MOTS-c itself. Its code sits in the DNA of mitochondria, inside the gene for 12S ribosomal RNA. A group at the University of Southern California first described it in 2015.
How it acts, according to animal and cell studies:

items.text: In cells, it slowed the folate cycle and purine production. That switched on AMPK, an enzyme that senses energy. Muscle appeared to be its main target.
In mice, it prevented insulin resistance caused by a high-fat diet or by age, and prevented diet-induced obesity.
In human blood in a test tube, it was broken into shorter pieces quickly. FDA says it is not known whether an injected dose reaches active levels in people.

src.label: Knoop et al., Rapid Commun Mass Spectrom, 2019

items.text: Exercise raised the body’s own MOTS-c in human muscle and blood.
FDA notes that its molecular target is unknown, so it is hard to predict which organs it affects.

what.text: None of these effects has been tested by giving MOTS-c to people.

research.text: Human evidence: none. FDA’s 2026 review found no published study in which MOTS-c was given to people by any route. One placebo-controlled trial is registered and has no results yet. Everything else is mouse, rat and cell work.
FDA searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, ClinicalTrials.gov and its adverse event database. It found no clinical studies or human exposure data.

research.title: A MOTS-c gene variant and long life (Japan)

facts.v: Fuku N, et al. Aging Cell 2015;14(6):921-3
short report. No one was given MOTS-c.
a variant (m.1382A>C) in the MOTS-c code, specific to Northeast Asian people

research.found: The authors suggest the variant may be one reason for long life in Japan. They say more research is needed.

items.text: male mice on a high-fat diet given daily injections for 8 weeks weighed about 20% less than untreated mice on the same diet, with less liver fat.

injections improved treadmill performance in young, middle-aged and old mice. In male mice treated three times a week from 23.5 months of age, median lifespan was 970 days against 912 untreated, and maximum lifespan 1,120 against 1,047 days. Two authors reported being consultants and shareholders of CohBar, Inc.
it raised bone-forming genes in rat bone stem cells, and reduced bone loss in the skulls of mice given plastic particles.
in rats given nicotine and vitamin D to calcify the aorta, it reduced calcification and heart changes.

research.text: FDA notes that all of this work was in rodents or cells, and none tested how effects change with dose. Animal results have not been confirmed in people.

items.text: FDA’s scientists, in a memo dated May 11, 2026 for the July meeting, recommended against adding MOTS-c (free base or acetate) to the compounding list. Reasons: it is not well characterized, its use in compounding is unknown, there are no animal toxicity data, and there are no human studies.

MOTS-c was nominated for insulin resistance, obesity, osteoporosis, vascular calcification, muscle and fat metabolism, and longevity. FDA said the nomination did not include enough information to evaluate any of these uses. The only nomination, from Wells Pharmacy Network, was withdrawn; FDA reviewed MOTS-c on its own initiative.

FDA’s advisory committee voted on MOTS-c on July 23, 2026: 7 in favor of adding it to the compounding list, 5 against and 2 abstaining, in both forms, as reported by Healio from the July 23–24, 2026 meeting. FDA has not posted the official vote record.

src.label: Healio, "FDA committee recommends looser restrictions for several peptides"

us.text: Not FDA-approved for any use. Since October 30, 2026, HHS has said it will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies and physicians that compound MOTS-c acetate for injection under the skin or into muscle, under set conditions. That is enforcement discretion, not approval. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: none. MOTS-c has no USP or National Formulary monograph and is not a component of any FDA-approved drug.

FDA lists MOTS-c among substances previously in Category 2 whose nominations were withdrawn. FDA wrote that it "may pose significant risk for immunogenicity" and that it found no human exposure data for any route.

HHS announced an enforcement discretion policy on October 28, 2026, published in the Federal Register on October 30, 2026 (Docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496). It names MOTS-c acetate, for injection under the skin or into muscle. HHS says it does not intend to take enforcement action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or licensed physicians that compound it when every condition is met. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: a licensed pharmacist or physician compounds it; the bulk substance matches the listed peptide and route; it comes from an FDA-registered maker that follows good manufacturing practice, with a valid certificate of analysis; there is a valid patient-specific prescription; the product contains only one active ingredient from the list; serious adverse events and quality problems are reported to FDA's MedWatch and state authorities; the label says "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."; oral forms have documented adequate bioavailability; the only device packaged with it is an FDA-cleared syringe; and all other section 503A requirements are met.

src.label: BakerHostetler summary of the HHS policy (a law firm's summary, used because HHS's own policy appendix could not be opened)

items.text: The policy does not make it FDA approved. It does not cover blends with other active ingredients, other routes or forms, outsourcing facilities (section 503B), or products sold as research chemicals or dietary supplements. It is interim and not binding: HHS may revise or withdraw it, in whole or in part, if safety signals or product-quality problems appear.

world.lead: No regulator has approved MOTS-c as a medicine. Canada names it among seized unauthorized peptides, EMA lists no MOTS-c medicine, and it is banned in sport at all times.

after.title: Sport
after.text: MOTS-c is named on the WADA Prohibited List under S4.4.1 (metabolic modulators: activators of AMPK). It is prohibited at all times, in and out of competition, and S4.4 substances are non-Specified. It stays named on the 2027 list, which takes effect January 1, 2027. An anti-doping lab in Cologne published a blood test for it in 2019.

src.label: Knoop et al., Rapid Commun Mass Spectrom, 2019

after.text: Australia: MOTS-c is not named in the Poisons Standard (June 2026). The TGA’s product register was not checked.

side.text: There are no human safety data. FDA found no studies in people and no animal toxicity studies, so its risks in people are unknown.

items.text: none. FDA found no clinical studies or human exposure data for any route.
searches of FAERS through March 9, 2025 found no reports. Compounding pharmacies generally do not report adverse events to FDA.
FDA found no single-dose, repeat-dose, genetic toxicity, reproductive or cancer studies.
FDA is concerned about immune reactions to injected MOTS-c, from clumping (aggregation) and peptide impurities. FDA says injection under the skin poses more of this risk than IV.
Health Canada warns that unauthorized injectable peptides may hold too much, too little or none of the ingredient, or contaminants such as bacteria, endotoxins or particles.

unconfirmed: UK (MHRA) status and Australia’s TGA product register were not checked against the regulator’s own record.
A completed Phase 1a/1b trial of CohBar’s CB4211 (NCT03998514) has no posted results, and its registry record does not describe CB4211 as MOTS-c, so it is left out.
Vote counts come from Healio's report of the July 23–24, 2026 meeting; FDA has not posted the official vote record.
surprises: MOTS-c is marketed for weight loss, insulin resistance, physical performance and slowing aging, but FDA found no published study in which it was given to a person by any route.
Lifespan claims trace to mice: the result FDA summarized was a median lifespan of 970 versus 912 days in male mice treated from old age.
MOTS-c is made by the body, yet WADA names it as a prohibited metabolic modulator, banned at all times.
In a test tube, human blood broke MOTS-c down quickly, and FDA says it is unknown whether injected MOTS-c reaches active levels in people.
It was nominated for six uses including longevity, but FDA said there was not enough information to evaluate any of them.
